sections.heading: What measurement means in chemistry
paragraphs: Every measured value has a number and a unit. Chemistry uses SI units: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K), mole (mol), and derived units such as litre (L) and pascal (Pa).
Prefixes scale units: kilo (k) = 10³, centi (c) = 10⁻², milli (m) = 10⁻³, micro (µ) = 10⁻⁶, nano (n) = 10⁻⁹. Dimensional analysis (cancel units) keeps conversions honest.

sections.heading: Significant figures
paragraphs: Significant figures (sig figs) show how precisely a value was measured. Non-zero digits always count. Zeros between digits count. Leading zeros never count. Trailing zeros count only if the decimal point is written (0.004050 has 4 sig figs; 4050 is ambiguous).
In multiplication and division, keep the fewest sig figs of any factor. In addition and subtraction, keep the fewest decimal places (least precise place).

worked.title: Sig figs in 0.004050
steps: Leading zeros before the first non-zero digit do not count → ignore 0.00
Digits that remain: 4, 0, 5, 0 → four significant figures

sections.heading: Density
paragraphs: Density ρ = m / V. Common units: g/mL or g/cm³ (same size for liquids and solids). Use density to convert mass ↔ volume.

worked.title: Density of a liquid
steps: ρ = 0.788 g/mL (3 sig figs; both inputs have 3)

sections.heading: Adding with the right precision
paragraphs: When you add or subtract, the answer stops at the least precise decimal place among the terms.

worked.title: 12.11 g + 18.0 g + 1.013 g
steps: Least precise term (18.0) is good only to the tenth place

sections.heading: Atoms and isotopes
paragraphs: An atom has protons (Z, atomic number) and neutrons in the nucleus, with electrons outside. Mass number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes of an element share Z but differ in neutrons.
For an ion, charge = protons − electrons. Example: ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ has Z = 26, so 26 protons, A − Z = 30 neutrons, and 26 − 3 = 23 electrons.

figure.note: Nuclear diagram of ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ showing protons, neutrons, and missing electrons

sections.heading: Average atomic mass
paragraphs: The periodic-table atomic mass is a weighted average of isotope masses: Σ (fraction × mass).

worked.title: Average atomic mass of Cl
steps: Isotopes: 75.78% ³⁵Cl (34.969 u) and 24.22% ³⁷Cl (36.966 u)

sections.heading: The mole
paragraphs: One mole contains Avogadro's number N_A ≈ 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Molar mass M (g/mol) equals the formula mass in u. n = m / M converts grams to moles.

worked.title: Moles of water in 10.0 g H₂O

sections.heading: Formulas and percent composition
paragraphs: An empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula. Mass percent of an element = (mass of element in 1 mol of compound / molar mass) × 100%.

worked.title: Mass % N in NH₄NO₃
steps: Mass of N in 1 mol = 2 × 14.01 = 28.02 g

sections.heading: Empirical formula from % composition
paragraphs: Assume 100 g of sample so % becomes grams. Convert each element to moles, divide by the smallest mole amount, and scale to whole numbers.

sections.heading: Molecular formula and oxidation states
paragraphs: If molar mass / empirical-formula mass = n, multiply subscripts by n. Example: CH₂O with M = 180 g/mol → n = 180/30 = 6 → C₆H₁₂O₆.
Oxidation state (oxidation number) is a bookkeeping charge: O is usually −2, H is +1 with nonmetals, elemental form is 0, and the sum equals the ion or molecule charge.

sections.heading: Balanced equations
paragraphs: A balanced chemical equation conserves atoms. Coefficients are mole ratios. Never change subscripts to balance — only coefficients.

worked.title: Balance and read mole ratios: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O
steps: Left: 4 H and 2 O; right: 4 H and 2 O — balanced
Mole ratio: 2 mol H₂ react with 1 mol O₂ to make 2 mol H₂O
Mass check (optional): 4.032 g H₂ + 32.00 g O₂ → 36.03 g H₂O

sections.heading: Limiting reactant and percent yield
paragraphs: Convert each reactant to moles of product using the mole ratio. The reactant that makes less product is limiting. Percent yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100%.

worked.title: 10.0 g H₂ + 64.0 g O₂ → water
steps: n(H₂) = 10.0/2.016 = 4.96 mol → can make 4.96 mol H₂O
n(O₂) = 64.0/32.00 = 2.00 mol → can make 4.00 mol H₂O
O₂ is limiting; theoretical mass H₂O = 4.00 × 18.02 = 72.1 g

sections.heading: Solution dilution
paragraphs: Molarity M = mol solute / L solution. Dilution conserves moles of solute: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.

worked.title: Dilute 25.0 mL of 6.00 M HCl to 150.0 mL

sections.heading: Light as energy packets
paragraphs: Light is electromagnetic radiation. Frequency ν and wavelength λ are linked by c = λν, with c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s. Photon energy E = hν = hc/λ, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.

sections.heading: The Bohr model for hydrogen
paragraphs: In hydrogen, electron energy levels are E_n = −13.6 eV / n². A jump from higher n to lower n emits a photon whose energy equals the level gap. The Balmer line n=3→2 is the famous red 656 nm line.

figure.note: Energy-level diagram for H showing n=1,2,3 and the n=3→2 photon

sections.heading: Orbitals and quantum numbers
paragraphs: Quantum numbers label orbitals: n (shell), ℓ (subshell: s,p,d,f), m_ℓ (orientation), m_s (spin ±½). An orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins (Pauli principle).

sections.heading: Building configurations
paragraphs: Fill orbitals in order of increasing energy (Aufbau): 1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 4s → 3d → 4p … Hund's rule: put one electron in each degenerate orbital before pairing.
Noble-gas shorthand writes the previous noble gas in brackets, then the remaining valence configuration. The block of the periodic table (s, p, d, f) matches the last subshell filled.

figure.note: Orbital box diagram for C and for N showing Hund's rule

worked.title: Find the element [Kr]4d¹⁰5s²5p³
steps: After Kr, add 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p³ → total electrons beyond Kr: 15

sections.heading: Exceptions and ions
paragraphs: Cr and Cu prefer half-filled or filled d subshells: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ (not 3d⁴4s²). For transition-metal cations, remove s electrons before d electrons: Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s²; Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵.

figure.note: Orbital box diagrams for Cr ([Ar]3d⁵4s¹) and Fe³⁺ ([Ar]3d⁵)

sections.heading: Atomic and ionic radius
paragraphs: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period (more protons pull the same shell tighter) and increases down a group (new shells). For isoelectronic ions (same electron count), more protons → smaller radius.

worked.title: Order Na⁺, Mg²⁺, F⁻, O²⁻ by increasing radius
steps: Nuclear charge: Mg 12 > Na 11 > F 9 > O 8
Higher Z pulls electrons closer → smaller ion

sections.heading: Ionization energy
paragraphs: First ionization energy (IE₁) generally rises across a period and falls down a group. Exceptions: Be→B and N→O. Removing a paired 2p electron from O is easier than removing an unpaired 2p electron from N because of electron–electron repulsion in the pair.

sections.heading: Paramagnetism
paragraphs: A species is paramagnetic if it has unpaired electrons. Ca ([Ar]4s²) and Zn²⁺ ([Ar]3d¹⁰) are diamagnetic; Fe²⁺ ([Ar]3d⁶) has unpaired electrons and is paramagnetic.

figure.note: Orbital box diagrams for Ca, Zn²⁺, and Fe²⁺ highlighting unpaired electrons

sections.heading: Lewis structures
paragraphs: Count valence electrons, connect atoms with single bonds, complete octets (H wants 2), and use multiple bonds or formal charge to refine. Formal charge = valence − (nonbonding e⁻) − ½(bonding e⁻).

figure.note: Lewis structures for H₂O, CO₂, and SF₄ (with lone pairs)

sections.heading: VSEPR shapes and polarity
paragraphs: Electron domains (bonds + lone pairs) arrange to minimize repulsion. Domains: 2 linear, 3 trigonal planar, 4 tetrahedral, 5 trigonal bipyramidal, 6 octahedral. Lone pairs take equatorial sites in TBP when possible.
Molecular shape ignores lone pairs for the name but includes them for angles. A molecule is polar if bond dipoles do not cancel.

figure.note: VSEPR shape of SF₄ (seesaw) with dipole arrow

worked.title: Shape and polarity of SF₄
steps: S has 6 valence e⁻; 4 F atoms → 4 bonds + 1 lone pair = 5 domains
Electron geometry: trigonal bipyramidal; molecular shape: seesaw
Lone pair and unsymmetric shape → dipoles do not cancel → polar

sections.heading: Bond enthalpies for reaction ΔH
paragraphs: Estimate ΔH ≈ Σ bonds broken − Σ bonds formed (using mean bond enthalpies). Breaking absorbs energy (+); forming releases (−).

worked.title: Estimate ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl
steps: Break 1 H–H and 1 Cl–Cl; form 2 H–Cl
Using typical mean values → about −184 kJ

sections.heading: Hybridization and σ / π bonds
paragraphs: Hybrid orbitals mix atomic orbitals to match the electron geometry: sp (linear), sp² (trigonal planar), sp³ (tetrahedral). A single bond is one σ bond. A double bond is σ + π; a triple is σ + 2π.

figure.note: Hybridization sketch for ethene (sp²) and ethyne (sp)

worked.title: σ and π bonds in CH₂=CH–C≡N
steps: Count all connections: C–H, C–C, C–C, C–N singles/multiples
Skeleton has 6 σ bonds (every single connection has one σ)
Double bond adds 1 π; triple bond adds 2 π → 3 π total

sections.heading: Molecular orbital (MO) theory
paragraphs: Atomic orbitals combine into bonding and antibonding MOs. Bond order = ½(bonding e⁻ − antibonding e⁻). Higher bond order → shorter, stronger bond. O₂ has two unpaired electrons in π* orbitals, so it is paramagnetic — Lewis structures miss this.

figure.note: MO energy diagram for O₂, O₂⁺, and O₂⁻ with electron filling

worked.title: Bond orders of O₂, O₂⁺, O₂⁻
steps: O₂ (12 valence e⁻ in MO count for O₂): bond order 2
O₂⁺ removes one antibonding e⁻ → bond order 2.5
O₂⁻ adds one antibonding e⁻ → bond order 1.5

sections.heading: Types of intermolecular forces
paragraphs: London dispersion: instantaneous dipoles; stronger for larger, more polarizable electron clouds and for longer contact area. Dipole–dipole: between permanent dipoles. Hydrogen bonding: H bonded to N, O, or F attracted to a lone pair on N, O, or F — unusually strong.
Stronger IMF → higher boiling/melting point (for similar molar mass).

worked.title: Boiling points: HF, Ne, HCl
steps: Ne: only weak dispersion → lowest bp

sections.heading: Shape matters
paragraphs: Straight-chain alkanes have more surface contact than branched isomers, so stronger dispersion and higher boiling points. Pentane boils higher than neopentane.

figure.note: Side-by-side sketches of pentane (chain) vs neopentane (compact)

sections.heading: Clausius–Clapeyron
paragraphs: Vapor pressure rises with T. ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁). Use absolute temperatures (K).

sections.heading: Gas laws and PV = nRT
paragraphs: Boyle: P ∝ 1/V at fixed n,T. Charles: V ∝ T (K). Avogadro: V ∝ n. Combined ideal-gas law: PV = nRT. Use consistent R (0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ when P in atm and V in L).

worked.title: P for 2.50 mol in 10.0 L at 25.0 °C

sections.heading: Molar mass and density
paragraphs: At the same T and P, equal volumes of ideal gases have equal moles (Avogadro). So denser gas = larger molar mass. CO₂ (44 g/mol) is denser than N₂ (28 g/mol) at the same T,P.

sections.heading: Partial pressures
paragraphs: Dalton's law: P_total = Σ P_i. Mole fraction x_i = n_i / n_total; P_i = x_i P_total.

sections.heading: Kinetic-molecular ideas
paragraphs: Gas pressure comes from collisions with the walls. Average translational KE per mole = (3/2)RT. Root-mean-square speed u_rms = √(3RT/M) with M in kg/mol.

sections.heading: Effusion and diffusion (Graham)
paragraphs: Rate of effusion ∝ 1/√M. Ratio of rates = √(M_heavy / M_light).

sections.heading: Real gases
paragraphs: Ideal gas ignores volume of molecules and attractions. At high P or low T, use van der Waals: (P + a n²/V²)(V − n b) = nRT. a corrects attractions; b corrects volume.

sections.heading: First law: ΔU = q + w
paragraphs: Internal energy U is a state function. Heat q into the system is positive; work w done on the system is positive in the chemistry sign convention used here (some physics texts flip w). For expansion work against constant P, w = −PΔV.

worked.title: System absorbs 250 J heat, does 100 J work
steps: w = −100 J (system does work on surroundings)

sections.heading: Enthalpy and calorimetry
paragraphs: H = U + PV. At constant pressure, q_p = ΔH. Coffee-cup calorimetry: q_sol ≈ −m c ΔT for the solution (sign flips for the reaction).

sections.heading: Hess's law and ΔH_f°
paragraphs: ΔH°_rxn = Σ n ΔH_f°(products) − Σ n ΔH_f°(reactants). Elements in standard state have ΔH_f° = 0.

worked.title: ΔH° for CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O(l)

sections.heading: K and Q
paragraphs: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b) at equilibrium. Q uses the same form with current concentrations. If Q < K, forward; Q > K, reverse; Q = K, at equilibrium.
K_p uses partial pressures in bar (or atm when that is the standard). K_p = K_c (RT)^{Δn} with Δn = moles gas products − reactants, and R = 0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ when pressures are in atm.

worked.title: K_p from K_c for N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃

sections.heading: ICE tables
paragraphs: Set Initial amounts, define Change with x using stoichiometry, write Equilibrium expressions, solve using K.

worked.title: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2 HI, K=49.0, start 0.0100 M each

sections.heading: Entropy
paragraphs: Entropy S measures dispersal of energy / number of microstates. Gases have much higher S than liquids or solids. Fewer gas moles → usually ΔS < 0. Standard entropy change: ΔS° = Σ n S°(products) − Σ n S°(reactants).

worked.title: Sign of ΔS for 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(l)

sections.heading: Gibbs energy
paragraphs: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (T in kelvin). Spontaneous as written when ΔG < 0. ΔG° = −RT ln K links thermodynamics to equilibrium. When ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, the reaction becomes spontaneous above T = ΔH/ΔS.

sections.heading: Rate laws and order
paragraphs: Rate = k [A]^m [B]^n … Orders m,n are found experimentally, not from stoichiometry. First-order: ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt; half-life t½ = ln 2 / k (constant).

sections.heading: Integrated first-order use
paragraphs: [A] = [A]₀ e^{−kt}. Plug in k and t to find remaining concentration.

sections.heading: Arrhenius equation
paragraphs: k = A e^{−Ea/RT}. From two temperatures: ln(k₂/k₁) = −(Ea/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).

worked.title: Ea when k doubles from 300 K to 310 K

sections.heading: Brønsted–Lowry and conjugates
paragraphs: Acid donates H⁺; base accepts H⁺. After transfer, the acid becomes its conjugate base and the base becomes its conjugate acid. Water can act as either (amphoteric).

worked.title: Conjugate pairs in NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻

sections.heading: Strong acids and pH
paragraphs: Strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ first proton, HClO₄) dissociate fully. For dilute strong monoprotic acid, [H₃O⁺] ≈ C_a; pH = −log[H₃O⁺].

sections.heading: Weak acids
paragraphs: For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, K_a = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. If x ≪ C_a, [H⁺] ≈ √(K_a C_a). Acetic acid K_a ≈ 1.8×10⁻⁵ (standard value; confirm against your table).

sections.heading: Buffers and Henderson–Hasselbalch
paragraphs: A buffer is a weak acid + its conjugate base (or weak base + conjugate acid). pH ≈ pK_a + log([A⁻]/[HA]). Best buffering when [A⁻]≈[HA] and both are reasonably concentrated.
sections.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 140" role="img" aria-label="Schematic titration curve (weak acid + strong base)"><text x="160.0" y="14" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1A1A1A">Schematic titration curve (weak acid + strong base)</text><path d="M 28.0,99.6 L 116.0,79.1 L 204.0,46.3 L 292.0,38.1" fill="none" stroke="#2B5FD9" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="28.0" cy="99.6" r="4" fill="#2B5FD9"/><circle cx="116.0" cy="79.1" r="4" fill="#2B5FD9"/><circle cx="204.0" cy="46.3" r="4" fill="#2B5FD9"/><circle cx="292.0" cy="38.1" r="4" fill="#2B5FD9"/><text x="28.0" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5F6B7A">start</text><text x="116.0" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5F6B7A">buffer</text><text x="204.0" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5F6B7A">eq.</text><text x="292.0" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5F6B7A">excess</text></svg>

sections.heading: Adding strong base to a buffer
paragraphs: OH⁻ converts HA → A⁻. Update the mole amounts, then reapply Henderson–Hasselbalch.

sections.heading: Equivalence point
paragraphs: For weak acid + strong base, the salt at equivalence is a weak base (A⁻), so pH > 7. Solve from K_b = K_w/K_a and the A⁻ concentration after dilution.

sections.heading: Electrolytes
paragraphs: Strong electrolytes dissociate fully (strong acids, strong soluble bases, soluble ionic salts). Weak electrolytes partially dissociate (weak acids/bases). Non-electrolytes (e.g. glucose, ethanol) dissolve as molecules.

sections.heading: Precipitation and net ionic equations
paragraphs: Write the full molecular equation, then the complete ionic equation, then cancel spectator ions to get the net ionic equation. Solubility rules decide which salts precipitate.

worked.title: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq)
steps: Ionic: Ag⁺ + NO₃⁻ + Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s) + Na⁺ + NO₃⁻

sections.heading: Redox in solution
paragraphs: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain. The oxidizing agent is reduced; the reducing agent is oxidized. In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, Cu²⁺ is the oxidizing agent and Zn is the reducing agent.

figure.note: Simple electron-transfer sketch: Zn metal and Cu²⁺ ions

sections.heading: K_sp
paragraphs: For M_mX_x(s) ⇌ m Mⁿ⁺ + x Xʸ⁻, K_sp = [M]^m [X]^x. Molar solubility s is the moles of solid that dissolve per litre.

worked.title: K_sp of CaF₂ from s = 2.1×10⁻⁴ M

sections.heading: Will it precipitate?
paragraphs: Compute Q with the mixed ion concentrations (after dilution). If Q > K_sp, precipitate forms; Q < K_sp, no precipitate; Q = K_sp, saturated.

worked.title: PbCl₂ after mixing
steps: Compare to K_sp(PbCl₂); Q < K_sp → no precipitate

sections.heading: Complex ions
paragraphs: Metal ions can bind ligands (NH₃, OH⁻, CN⁻…) to form complex ions, which can raise the apparent solubility of a precipitate (e.g. AgCl in NH₃).

sections.heading: Half-reaction method (acidic)
paragraphs: Split into oxidation and reduction half-reactions. Balance atoms other than O and H, then O with H₂O, then H with H⁺, then charge with e⁻. Multiply to equalize electrons and add.

worked.title: MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ (acidic)
steps: Reduction: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺; add 4 H₂O, 8 H⁺, 5 e⁻
Add: MnO₄⁻ + 5 Fe²⁺ + 8 H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5 Fe³⁺ + 4 H₂O

sections.heading: Basic solution
paragraphs: Balance as if acidic, then add OH⁻ to both sides to neutralize H⁺, forming water, and cancel extra H₂O.

worked.title: MnO₄⁻ + I⁻ → MnO₂ + I₂ (basic)
steps: Acidic balance first, then convert H⁺ to H₂O with OH⁻
Result: 2 MnO₄⁻ + 6 I⁻ + 4 H₂O → 2 MnO₂ + 3 I₂ + 8 OH⁻

sections.heading: Redox titration
paragraphs: Use the balanced electron ratio to relate moles of titrant to analyte. Example: 1 MnO₄⁻ oxidizes 5 Fe²⁺ in acid.

sections.heading: Galvanic cells
paragraphs: A galvanic (voltaic) cell runs a spontaneous redox reaction to make electric current. Oxidation at the anode; reduction at the cathode. E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode (using reduction potentials).

figure.note: Zn|Zn²⁺||Cu²⁺|Cu galvanic cell diagram with anode, cathode, salt bridge

worked.title: E° for Zn–Cu cell
steps: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V; E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V (standard table values)

sections.heading: ΔG°, K, and E°
paragraphs: ΔG° = −n F E°_cell. Positive E°_cell means ΔG° < 0 and K > 1 (products favored at standard state).

sections.heading: Nernst equation
paragraphs: At 25 °C: E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q. Lower [product ions] / higher [reactant ions] raises E for the forward cell reaction.

sections.heading: Absorption and energy
paragraphs: Molecules absorb photons that match an allowed energy gap. E = hc/λ per photon; multiply by N_A for per-mole energy. Longer λ → smaller energy.

sections.heading: IR and wavenumbers
paragraphs: Infrared often reported as wavenumber ν̃ = 1/λ (cm⁻¹). Bond vibrations: stronger/lighter bonds → higher wavenumber.

sections.heading: Conjugation and color
paragraphs: In conjugated π systems, the HOMO–LUMO gap shrinks as the chain lengthens, so λ_max moves to longer wavelength (bathochromic shift). Enough conjugation and the absorption enters the visible — the compound looks colored.

figure.note: HOMO–LUMO gap sketch for short vs long conjugated chain
